title: Budget Stabilization Fund
plainSummary: A YES vote raises the cap on Florida's rainy-day fund (the Budget Stabilization Fund) from 10% to 25% of general revenue and requires the Legislature to deposit the lesser of $750 million or the amount needed to reach 25% every year. Withdrawals would be limited to emergencies, revenue shortfalls, or a 'critical state need' approved by two-thirds of both chambers once the fund exceeds 15%.
origin: Placed by the 2025 Florida Legislature via House Joint Resolution 5019, sponsored by Rep. Lawrence McClure (R-Dover). Passed the House 100-1 and the Senate 29-4; joint resolutions need three-fifths of each chamber and no governor's signature.
fiscalImpact: No Financial Impact Estimating Conference statement (legislative referral, not a citizen initiative). Vote411/LWV summary: fiscal impact on the state 'indeterminate, but likely insignificant.' Florida TaxWatch: current BSF balance about $5.06B (9.75% of GR); at steady growth the 25% target would not be reached until about 2049 after roughly $16.4B in added deposits.
supporters: Senate President Ben Albritton, House Speaker Daniel Perez, Rep. Lawrence McClure, Republican Party of Florida, Florida TaxWatch (calls it 'a very tough call' but recommends Yes), Pinellas County Republican Party slate (Yes); Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly reportedly backs it with 'guardrails'
opponents: Gov. Ron DeSantis ('a foolish constitutional amendment proposal', 'a solution in search of a problem'), Americans for Tax Reform, Florida Education Association, League of Women Voters of Florida, Florida AFL-CIO (raised concerns), House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell (concerns, though she voted for it); Pinellas Democratic-aligned Voter Action Pinellas guide recommends No
argumentsFor: Supporters say a larger constitutionally protected reserve prepares Florida for recessions, hurricanes and federal funding shocks without tax hikes or service cuts, and that the current 10% cap is too low for a $100B+ budget. Speaker Perez cited the state's unpreparedness in the 2000s recession.
argumentsAgainst: DeSantis argues reserves are already at the cap with large surpluses and the money should go to tax cuts instead. Democrats, FEA and LWV say locking away up to $750M a year for decades diverts money from unmet needs ('saving for a rainy day when it's still raining'), and TaxWatch itself worries the mandatory transfer could run for a very long time.
polling: Stetson University (Oct 1-9, 2026, 716 RV, released Oct 13): 46% yes / 30% no / 23% undecided. James Madison Institute/Targoz (Sept 28-Oct 4, 2026, n=1,125 RV, MOE 2.77): 40% yes / 32% no / 28% undecided. Both well short of 60%.
pinellasNote: No direct local fiscal effect; the fund is a state reserve. Statewide polling suggests it is unlikely to reach 60%.

title: Exemption of Tangible Personal Property on Agricultural Land from Taxation
plainSummary: A YES vote exempts farm equipment, machinery and other tangible personal property that is habitually kept on land classified as agricultural, used for farming or agritourism, and owned by the landowner or leaseholder, from local property taxes. It would first apply to the 2027 tax year.
origin: Placed by the 2025 Florida Legislature via House Joint Resolution 1215 (House sponsor not confirmed in sources reviewed; championed publicly by Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson). Passed the House 110-1 (Rep. Anna Eskamani the lone no) and the Senate 37-0.
fiscalImpact: No Financial Impact Estimating Conference statement (legislative referral). Legislature's Revenue Estimating Conference: negative recurring impact on local government revenue of about $31.0M in FY2027-28, $32.3M in FY2028-29 and $33.6M in FY2029-30; roughly $1.685B in taxable agricultural TPP across about 18,900 accounts statewide.
supporters: Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson, Florida Farm Bureau Federation, Florida TaxWatch (Yes), Pinellas County Republican Party slate (Yes)
opponents: Rep. Anna Eskamani, League of Women Voters of Florida, Florida Education Association; Voter Action Pinellas (Democratic-aligned) recommends No. No organized campaign on either side.
argumentsFor: Supporters say the tangible personal property tax is costly to comply with and administer, penalizes investment in equipment, and squeezes farmers already hit by hurricanes, citrus disease and development pressure. TaxWatch calls the local revenue loss relatively small.
argumentsAgainst: Opponents say it strips about $31M a year from counties, cities and school districts with no means test, mostly benefiting large agribusinesses with multiple TPP accounts, and that tax carve-outs do not belong in the constitution. The hit would be larger for small rural counties, especially if Amendment 3 also passes.
polling: Stetson University (Oct 1-9, 2026, released Oct 13): 56% yes / 21% no / 23% undecided. James Madison Institute/Targoz (Sept 28-Oct 4, 2026, n=1,077 RV): 53% yes / 20% no / 28% undecided. Closest of the three to 60% but still short.
pinellasNote: Pinellas is heavily urbanized with little classified agricultural land, so the direct local revenue effect would be minimal compared with rural counties.

title: Increased Homestead Exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non-Homestead Property Assessments
plainSummary: A YES vote raises the homestead exemption for all non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 (indexed to inflation after that), for people who are Florida residents by Dec. 31, 2026; newcomers wait until their fifth year. It also cuts the annual assessment-increase cap on non-homestead property (rentals, businesses, second homes) from 10% to 5%, lets counties and cities later exempt homesteads entirely, and restricts what counties and cities may spend property taxes on.
origin: Placed by the Legislature in a June 1-3, 2026 special session as CS/HJR 1F ('Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes'), House sponsor Rep. Toby Overdorf, Senate companion SJR 2F by Sen. Bryan Avila, at Gov. DeSantis's urging. Passed June 2, 2026: House 75-26 (reported as 75-27 with 16 not voting by LWV), Senate 30-9 (3 Democrats yes, 2 Republicans no). On Aug. 4-5, 2026 Leon Circuit Judge David Frank ruled the original title/summary misleading; AG James Uthmeier issued the rewritten title now on the ballot on Aug. 13, 2026. The state did not appeal.
fiscalImpact: No Financial Impact Estimating Conference statement (legislative referral). Revenue Estimating Conference (June 12, 2026): local non-school property tax revenue falls about $4.95B in FY2027-28, $8.78B in FY2028-29, rising to about $11.86B recurring by FY2031-32; Florida TaxWatch five-year total $45.8B. Counties bear roughly $2.7B of the first-year loss. No replacement state revenue is provided. At the statewide average 10.5 non-school mills an average homestead saves about $1,035 in 2027 and $2,085 in 2028. Moody's, Fitch and S&P all warn of credit pressure on local governments.
supporters: Gov. Ron DeSantis, Florida Realtors (sole funder of the 'Vote Yes on 3' committee: $18M reported in September, about $19.5M by late October), Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds, Rep. Toby Overdorf, Sen. Bryan Avila, Pinellas County Republican Party slate, Pinellas Watchdogs (local Substack)
opponents: Florida Association of Counties, Florida League of Cities, Florida Sheriffs Association, Florida Fraternal Order of Police, Florida Professional Firefighters, Florida Fire Chiefs Association, Florida TaxWatch, Florida Policy Institute, Tax Foundation, 1000 Friends of Florida, League of Women Voters of Florida, Florida Education Association, Florida AFL-CIO, SEIU Florida, Florida PTA, NAACP Florida, 'Floridians for Shared Prosperity' and 'Vote No On 3' committees (combined about $680K), Senate President Ben Albritton and former Senate President Kathleen Passidomo (both voting no), Pinellas County Democratic Party, Pinellas Sheriff Bob Gualtieri (warned of cuts), editorial boards of the Tampa Bay Times, Miami Herald, Orlando Sentinel, Palm Beach Post, Sun-Sentinel, Wall Street Journal and Washington Post
argumentsFor: Supporters call it the largest property tax cut in state history: a home assessed at $250,000 or less would pay no non-school property tax by 2028, and the 5% cap protects landlords and businesses from assessment spikes. DeSantis and the Realtors argue homeowners should not pay 'rent to the government,' that local budgets have ballooned with rising values, and that the spending-purpose list forces cities and counties to prioritize police, fire and infrastructure.
argumentsAgainst: Opponents say it is a tax shift, not a cut: roughly $12B a year vanishes from county and city budgets with no replacement, forcing cuts to police, fire, transit, libraries and parks or higher millage, fees and special assessments that fall on renters (about 3 million households get nothing) and businesses. They also cite the five-year wait for new residents (equal-protection concerns; a similar provision was struck in 1982), the rushed one-week special session, the court finding that the ballot language was misleading, and the loss of local control over spending.
polling: Every October poll is below 60%. UNF Public Opinion Research Lab (Oct 12-19, 2026, n=1,471 LV, MOE 2.81): 50% yes / 30% no / 14% undecided. NBC6/SurveyUSA-type poll (Sept 28-Oct 1, 625 RV): 55% yes. Stetson (Oct 1-9, released Oct 13): 56% yes / 21% no / 23% undecided. AIF Center for Political Strategy (mid-Oct): 53% yes, short of 60% in every media market. EDGE/MDW: 50/27/23. James Madison Institute/Targoz (Sept 28-Oct 4, n=1,151): 59% yes / 22% no / 19% undecided (63% among likely voters, the only poll near the threshold). St. Pete Polls for Florida Politics (October): about 42% support. Florida Chamber CEO Mark Wilson said it will be 'pretty hard to get to 60%.'
pinellasNote: Pinellas is among the hardest-hit counties: Florida TaxWatch ranks it sixth statewide with about $2.31B in lost local property tax revenue over five years. Property Appraiser analysis projects taxable value falling roughly $36B and the county general fund losing more than 24%, about $164M, by 2030; county staff earlier briefed commissioners on losses of about $124M in 2028 and $184M in 2029, and Sheriff Gualtieri estimated a $180M first-year general fund hit. About 66% of Pinellas residential parcels are homesteaded. City estimates: St. Petersburg $33M (FY28) and $54M (FY29), nearly 25% of the revenue that funds 92% of its public safety budget; Clearwater about $12M then $20M+ cumulative, with a memo citing 140 positions and the Beach Library; Largo $15.7M (property taxes are 60% of its general fund). PSTA could lose about a quarter of its operating funding (Tampa Bay Times, Oct 26). Former Sen. Jeff Brandes predicted Pinellas could consolidate from 24 cities to about 18 within five to seven years. Note that a YES on Amendment 3 also raises the share of the St. Pete $600M bond tax borne by higher-value and non-homestead properties.

title: Removing the Requirement the Town Commission Appoint a Planning and Zoning Board
plainSummary: A YES vote deletes Charter Section 5.04, which requires the Town Commission to appoint a planning and zoning board. The town would still have a local planning agency because Florida law (s. 163.3174) already requires one; the charter language is considered redundant.
origin: Recommended by the town's 2026 Charter Review Committee; Ordinance 597 passed first reading at a July 14, 2026 Town Commission special meeting (Legistar file 26-0072) and was adopted to place the question on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot. Vote tally not published online.
supporters: Belleair Charter Review Committee, town staff (recommended approval)
argumentsFor: The planning and zoning board is the only board the charter mandates, and state law already compels the town to maintain a local planning agency, so the provision is unnecessary duplication.
argumentsAgainst: A no vote keeps an explicit charter guarantee that the town maintain an appointed planning and zoning board rather than relying only on state statute.

title: Amending the Month the Charter Review Committee is Established
plainSummary: A YES vote changes Charter Section 10.01 so the decennial Charter Review Committee is formed in May instead of June, starting in 2036. The extra month gives the committee time to finish its work and lets the town meet the Supervisor of Elections' deadlines for placing amendments on the following November ballot.
origin: Recommended by the 2026 Charter Review Committee and placed on the ballot by Town Commission ordinance in summer 2026 alongside Charter Amendment No. 1. Ordinance number and vote tally not published online.
supporters: Belleair Charter Review Committee, town staff
argumentsFor: The 2026 committee found the June start left too little time to review the charter and get ballot language to the county before the general-election deadline.
argumentsAgainst: None identified; a no vote keeps the June start date.

title: Change of Date when Petitions for Candidates for Mayor and City Commission are First Available
plainSummary: A YES vote amends Charter Section 7.02(a) so that nominating petitions for mayor and city commission candidates become available on March 15 of each regular election year (or a date the commission sets for a special election), instead of 45 days before qualifying opens. Candidates still need 200 registered-voter signatures.
origin: City Commission direction at a March 11, 2025 discussion (consensus to keep the 200-card requirement but start distribution March 15), enacted as Ordinance No. 2025-24 placing the question on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot. Adoption date and vote tally not found online.
supporters: Largo City Commission; Voter Action Pinellas (Democratic-aligned guide) recommends Yes
argumentsFor: Gives candidates several more months to gather the 200 petition signatures, lowering the barrier to running for city office.
argumentsAgainst: A no vote keeps the shorter 45-day window; some argue a longer petition season lengthens campaigns.

title: Change Municipal Election Date from March to November
plainSummary: A YES vote moves Madeira Beach's regular city elections from March to November so they coincide with the state general election. Staff say a stand-alone March election costs the city about $7,000 versus roughly $300 to piggyback on the November ballot, and November turnout is historically far higher.
origin: Staff proposal discussed at a June 24, 2026 workshop; Ordinance 2026-18 passed first reading July 8, 2026 (4-0) and final adoption Oct. 14, 2026 by a 4-0 vote (Commissioner Chuck Dillon absent), per The Gabber; a Citizen Portal account dates the election call to Sept. 9 (5-0). Placed as one of three linked amendments.
fiscalImpact: Saves roughly $6,700 per election cycle (about $7,000 for a March election vs. about $300 in November), per city staff.
supporters: Madeira Beach Board of Commissioners (unanimous), city staff
argumentsFor: Higher turnout, lower cost, and alignment with county, state and federal elections; several Pinellas beach towns have made or are making the same move.
argumentsAgainst: City races can get lost at the bottom of a long November ballot, and the companion Amendment No. 3 extends current officials' terms by up to 20 months without an election.

title: Change Candidate Qualifying Period from December to June
plainSummary: A YES vote moves the candidate qualifying window from the first two full weeks of December to the first two full weeks of June (weekdays only), to fit a November election calendar. It is a companion to Amendment No. 1.
origin: Same Ordinance 2026-18 adopted by the Board of Commissioners (first reading July 8, 2026; final adoption Oct. 14, 2026, 4-0).
supporters: Madeira Beach Board of Commissioners, city staff
argumentsFor: Needed mechanically if elections move to November; June qualifying matches the county's ballot-certification timeline.
argumentsAgainst: Only makes sense if Amendment No. 1 passes; a December qualifying period would be meaningless for a November election.

title: Extend Terms of Elected Officials to Implement November Elections
plainSummary: A YES vote temporarily extends sitting officials' terms to bridge from March to November elections: District 3 and District 4 commissioners serve until the November 2027 results are certified, and the Mayor-Commissioner and District 1 and 2 commissioners serve until the November 2028 results are certified. Future terms return to normal length.
origin: Same Ordinance 2026-18 (first reading July 8, 2026; final adoption Oct. 14, 2026, 4-0, Commissioner Dillon absent).
supporters: Madeira Beach Board of Commissioners, city staff
argumentsFor: A one-time extension avoids a stand-alone transitional election and lets every future election fall in November.
argumentsAgainst: Incumbents extend their own terms by roughly eight months (2027 seats) to 20 months (2028 seats) without facing voters; Tampa Bay Business & Wealth noted this is the part most likely to draw attention.

title: Commissioners' Term of Office
plainSummary: A YES vote lengthens district commissioners' terms from two years to three. Under the ordinance, Districts 2 and 4 would get three-year terms starting with the 2027 election and Districts 1 and 3 starting in 2028, keeping staggered seats.
origin: Board of Commissioners Ordinance ORD2026-01 (after discussion in Nov. 2025, Jan. 2026 and a Feb. 25, 2026 workshop), passed first reading March 2026 and adopted on second reading April 8, 2026 by a 5-0 vote. A companion ORD2026-02 moves town elections to November. In Nov. 2025 some residents urged delay for more public education.
fiscalImpact: Fewer elections over time; the town says reducing election frequency saves cost. No dollar figure given.
supporters: Redington Shores Board of Commissioners (unanimous), modeled on neighboring Indian Shores
opponents: None organized identified; residents at a Nov. 2025 meeting asked for more public notice
argumentsFor: The ordinance finds three-year terms let commissioners 'better serve their constituents' and reduce the frequency of elections in a town of about 4,400 people.
argumentsAgainst: Longer terms mean voters get fewer chances to replace commissioners; the proposal moved through with little public comment.

title: Mayoral 2027 Term of Office
plainSummary: A YES vote, effective only if Question No. 1 passes, makes the mayoral term elected in 2027 a one-time two-year term (instead of three) so the mayor's election stays staggered from the commissioners' new three-year cycle. From 2029 the mayor returns to three-year terms.
origin: Same Ordinance ORD2026-01, adopted April 8, 2026, 5-0. The commission tabled an earlier draft in February 2026 specifically to clarify how the mayor's cycle would align.
argumentsFor: Keeps the mayor and commissioners from all coming up for election in the same year.
argumentsAgainst: Adds complexity; moot if Question No. 1 fails.

title: Stormwater, Wastewater and/or Potable Water Improvements General Obligation Bond Referendum
plainSummary: A YES vote lets the city borrow up to $600 million in general obligation bonds, repaid by a new voter-approved property tax, to speed up St. Pete Agile Resilience (SPAR) projects: flood protection, stormwater pump stations and drainage, sewage collection and treatment hardening, and drinking-water supply and distribution. The city says it would finish its $2.7 billion priority list in about 19 years instead of 24.
origin: St. Petersburg City Council approved the ballot language 7-0 on July 23, 2026 (Council member Gina Driscoll absent), following the 2024 Helene and Milton flooding and sewage plant shutdowns. Bonds would be issued in series from 2027 to 2030, each maturing within 30 years.
fiscalImpact: City estimate: about 0.96 mills, roughly $96 a year per $100,000 of taxable value at full issuance (about $288 a year on a home with $300,000 taxable value), assuming 4.5% interest over 30 years; payments start lower as bonds are issued incrementally. More than half of the $600M is for protecting water and wastewater utilities from storm surge. If it fails, the same work continues pay-as-you-go through utility rates over a longer timeline. If Amendment 3 passes, more of the bond levy shifts to higher-value and non-homestead properties.
supporters: Mayor Ken Welch, City Council (unanimous), Tampa Bay Times editorial board, Creative Loafing, Suncoast Sierra Club, Council of Neighborhood Associations (CONA), Voter Action Pinellas (Democratic-aligned guide); St. Petersburg Area Chamber of Commerce takes no position
opponents: Mayoral challenger Charlie Crist (says he will vote no, citing affordability and city debt capacity; prefers not adding GO bonds); League of Women Voters of the St. Petersburg Area, Sierra Club and CONA pressed for more spending transparency without opposing it
argumentsFor: The 2024 hurricanes exposed decades of under-investment; borrowing now locks in construction costs before inflation, delivers flood protection five years sooner, and keeps sewage plants running during storms. Welch says most homeowners with taxable value of $500,000 or less come out ahead versus funding it through utility rate hikes, which hit every ratepayer regardless of value.
argumentsAgainst: Crist and other critics say residents are already squeezed by insurance and tax increases, the city is taking on too much debt, and the property-tax route is regressive for owners of higher-value homes compared with utility rates. Civic groups wanted an earlier, clearer project list and ongoing accounting of how the money is spent.
polling: St. Pete Polls for Florida Politics (late Oct 2026, likely St. Petersburg voters): about 45% support / 21% oppose / 35% undecided; among those who had already voted, 52% yes / 23% no.
pinellasNote: Applies only to St. Petersburg property owners. The new levy would come on top of the city's existing millage and is separate from statewide Amendment 3, which would cut the city's general property tax revenue by an estimated $33M in FY28 and $54M in FY29.

title: Removing City-Owned Vacant Lots from Park and Waterfront Map to Create Housing
plainSummary: A YES vote removes nine vacant, fenced-off city-owned lots (about 1.7 acres) next to the Jamestown Apartments near Burlington Avenue N from the charter's voter-protected Park and Waterfront Map, so the city can rezone and sell or partner on them for affordable or workforce housing. Unity Park and the Jamestown open space stay protected.
origin: City bought the lots under a 1982 redevelopment plan as a buffer; that requirement expired in 2012 but the parcels were locked in by the 1984 voter-approved map. The Housing, Land Use and Transportation Committee voted unanimously March 12, 2026 to advance it, and City Council placed it on the ballot unanimously in July 2026 as part of a five-question package.
fiscalImpact: No tax impact. Staff estimate four small lots could go to the Affordable Lot Disposition Program for single-family homes and five larger parcels could yield about 37 affordable/workforce units through an RFP; proceeds and subsidy would be decided later.
supporters: City Council and city housing staff, Tampa Bay Times editorial board (Yes), Voter Action Pinellas (Democratic-aligned, Yes)
opponents: Creative Loafing (recommends No), Pinellas County Republican Party slate (No), Methodist Town Neighborhood Association members who said they had no say and proposed a community garden or green space; Council Vice Chair Richie Floyd objected to putting city land in private hands
argumentsFor: The lots have never functioned as parks, are closed to the public, attract illegal dumping and have sat idle for 40 years; the city badly needs affordable housing and downtown-adjacent land is scarce.
argumentsAgainst: Opponents distrust removing any parcels from the voter-protected park map, want the land kept in public hands or used as neighborhood green space, and say the ballot language is broad enough to allow outright sale to private developers.

title: Authorizing Amendment of Harborage Marina Lease to Extend Term to 30 Years and Require Improvements
plainSummary: A YES vote lets City Council extend the Harborage Marina's lease of city-owned submerged land in Bayboro Harbor from the 22 years remaining to a fresh 30-year term, under conditions in Ordinance 640-H. In exchange the tenant must build about $2.15 million of improvements at its own cost (200 linear feet of docks, boat lifts, expanded restrooms), which the city owns when the lease ends.
origin: City Council unanimously approved the ordinance on first reading July 9, 2026 and placed it on the Nov. 3 ballot; the charter requires voter approval for long-term waterfront leases. Even with voter approval, Council must still adopt a final resolution.
fiscalImpact: No cost to the city; marina-funded $2.15M in improvements. City staff estimate about $4.5M in additional lease revenue over the term (the marina's own estimate is $3.5M over 30 years).
supporters: Harborage Marina, City Council (unanimous), Tampa Bay Times editorial board ('a classic win-win'), Creative Loafing, St. Petersburg Area Chamber of Commerce, Innovation District CEO Alison Barlow, Voter Action Pinellas
opponents: Pinellas County Republican Party slate (No, no reason given); no organized opposition
argumentsFor: Lenders require a longer term before financing upgrades; the city gets new docks and facilities for free, more rent, and keeps ownership.
argumentsAgainst: Extends a private operator's control of public submerged land by eight more years; skeptics of long waterfront leases generally prefer shorter terms.

title: Authorizing a 25-year Lease Limitation for the Port of St. Petersburg
plainSummary: A YES vote raises the maximum lease term the city may sign at the Port of St. Petersburg without a citywide referendum from 10 years to 25 years, matching the limit voters set for adjacent Albert Whitted Airport in 2004. It does not approve any specific lease or change the port's permitted uses; each deal still needs Council approval.
origin: Proposed by the Welch administration in early 2026 (Tampa Bay Times, Feb. 26, 2026) and placed on the ballot by City Council in July 2026 as part of the five-question package. Driven by the Maritime and Defense Technology Hub's federal grant application for a planned 50,000-square-foot Center for Coastal Resilience, which requires a 25-year site commitment.
fiscalImpact: No direct cost; the city says longer leases would attract private investment and grant funding for port redevelopment.
supporters: City administration and Council, Innovation District CEO Alison Barlow, St. Petersburg Area Chamber of Commerce, Tampa Bay Times editorial board, Creative Loafing, St. Pete Rising (op-ed), Voter Action Pinellas
opponents: Pinellas County Republican Party slate (No, no reason given); no organized opposition
argumentsFor: Ten-year terms scare off funders and tenants who need assurance a project will last; Barlow says the Hub may lose federal grants without a 25-year commitment. The airport has operated under the same 25-year rule for two decades without problems.
argumentsAgainst: Waterfront-protection advocates prefer keeping voters in the loop on long leases of public waterfront; a 25-year deal with a private developer locks the port's use for a generation.

title: Technical, Clarifying, and Conforming Changes to Effectuate Holding Municipal Elections in Even-Numbered Years
plainSummary: A YES vote cleans up leftover charter language from the 2022 voter-approved move of mayor and council elections to even-numbered years (first held in 2024), including re-timing the charter review process so it lines up with the new election calendar. It makes no substantive policy change.
origin: Placed on the ballot by City Council in July 2026 as part of the five-question package; staff identified conforming changes not made in the 2022 amendment.
supporters: City Council, Tampa Bay Times editorial board, Creative Loafing, Voter Action Pinellas
opponents: Pinellas County Republican Party slate (No, no reason given)
argumentsFor: Housekeeping needed to fully implement what voters already approved; avoids ambiguity about when the next charter review commission is convened.
argumentsAgainst: None substantive identified; the Republican slate's blanket No appears to be general opposition to the city's charter package.

title: Shall Charter be Amended Requiring Four Commissioners' Approval for Planned Developments or Special Area Plans
plainSummary: A YES vote amends Charter Section 3.07(c) to require a supermajority of four of the five commissioners (instead of a simple majority of three) to approve any planned development or special area plan. It would take effect immediately, giving residents a higher bar against large redevelopment projects.
origin: Citizen initiative led by resident Mark Hohe amid the post-hurricane debate over a new Planned Development (PD) zoning ordinance; the Supervisor of Elections certified sufficient petition signatures in July 2026 and the City Commission voted Aug. 5, 2026 to place it on the ballot. The city attorney advised it could face a legal challenge after the election but was proper for referendum.
supporters: Petition organizer Mark Hohe, Local Planning Agency member Grant Smith and other residents worried about height and density; Commissioners Arden Dickey and Chris Clark voiced concern that the PD ordinance lacks guardrails
opponents: Developer representatives (Lauren Rubenstein for the Thunderbird property opposed a supermajority); Vice Mayor Tammy Vasquez pushed a narrower alternative requiring four votes only when a project seeks both maximum height (80 ft) and density (100 units/acre)
argumentsFor: Hohe argues a simple-majority PD process lets three commissioners approve projects far taller and denser than the beach community wants, and that Vasquez's narrower trigger could be dodged by proposing just under the maximums.
argumentsAgainst: Opponents say a blanket supermajority makes an already expensive PD process riskier for property owners trying to rebuild after Helene and Milton, deters investment, and that county height and density limits already apply.
